# Results — Study 43 (Free-Lunch): betting against beta on a liquid-ETF cross-section, 2000–2026

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Daily returns of **13 liquid ETFs**
spanning the beta spectrum (XLU/XLP/XLV/TLT/IEF/GLD … XLK/XLY/XLF/XLE/XLI/IWM/EEM) with **SPY** as the
market and **^IRX** (13-week T-bill) as the cash rate. Beta-neutral BAB: long the low-beta half
(levered to beta 1), short the high-beta half, rebalanced monthly, **self-financed** — borrowed slice
at rf + spread, short rebate at rf − fee, every dollar charged once. Every Sharpe below is
**excess-of-cash**, BAB and market alike. As-of **2026-06-01** (complete months only); inputs
fingerprint `482c3b72db16`.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `WEAK` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · "Free lunch"? `BUSTED`

Priced honestly, the famous factor trails the index it claims to beat: the self-financed BAB book's
gross excess Sharpe is **0.32** against SPY's **0.48** — and that 0.32 already assumes you finance
2.77× leverage at the T-bill flat, with free stock borrow. Charge realistic frictions *on top of* rf
and what's left goes too: net Sharpe **0.23** at a 1% financing spread, **0.09** at 2.5%, **negative
past ~3.5%**. And the book's apparently strong early years were substantially a **levered duration/gold
trade**, not the intra-equity low-risk anomaly: the gross book correlates **+0.55 with TLT**, and the
intra-equity-only version (drop TLT/IEF/GLD) earns a flat, small **0.21** with **no decay**. The "low-risk
anomaly that beats the market" is `BUSTED` as a free lunch — **the lunch is the leverage bill**, the
same mechanism Study 30 (House-Edge) found for levered dip-buying.

## Data stamp

- **Cross-section**: 13 ETFs + SPY + ^IRX, 2000-01 → 2026-05, 317 months, fingerprint `482c3b72db16`
- **Average long-leg leverage**: 2.77× · **average T-bill**: 1.9%/yr over the sample

## BAB vs the market, excess of cash

| | CAGR | Sharpe (excess) | vol | max-DD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BAB gross (self-financed, zero spreads) | +6.6% | **0.32** | 21.6% | −47% |
| BAB net (spread 1% + borrow fee 0.25%) | +4.5% | **0.23** | 21.7% | −51% |
| BAB net (spread 2.5% + borrow fee 0.5%) | +1.5% | **0.09** | 21.7% | −57% |
| **SPY (the market)** | +8.3% | **0.48** | 15.2% | −51% |

*(BAB rows are the funded book — capital at rf plus the long-short P&L — so the CAGRs are
apples-to-apples with SPY; all four Sharpes are measured against the same T-bill.)*

Two things at once. First, **even gross, the honestly-constructed book trails the market: 0.32 vs
0.48**. The old trick that made BAB look close was comparing a raw long-short return (which quietly
pockets free funding on its net-long notional, worth ≈ rf × 1.9 ≈ 3.6%/yr here) to a raw SPY return
(which still carries its cash hurdle). Measure both legs in excess of the same T-bill — the Frazzini &
Pedersen construction itself — and the gap is plain. Second, the 2.77× leverage means every basis point
of financing spread is amplified: the sweep below shows the edge bleeding to zero.

## The financing sweep — where the residual edge goes

| financing spread over rf (borrow fee = spread/4) | net Sharpe |
|---|---|
| 0% | +0.32 |
| 1% | +0.23 |
| 2% | +0.13 |
| 3% | +0.04 |
| 4% | −0.05 |

The low-beta leg has β ≈ 0.36, so it must be held at **1/0.36 ≈ 2.8×** to reach beta 1. Frazzini &
Pedersen's thesis is that leverage-constrained investors *bid up* high-beta assets, leaving a premium
for those willing to lever the low-beta ones — but that premium is **the rent on the leverage**. A
retail margin markup (~2.5% over bills, the Study 30 central case) keeps less than a third of the
gross Sharpe; past ~3.5% the book compounds negatively.

## What the long leg actually is — the duration confound

| | gross Sharpe | leverage | corr with TLT |
|---|---|---|---|
| Full 13-ETF book | 0.32 | 2.77× | **+0.55** |
| Intra-equity only (drop TLT/IEF/GLD) | 0.21 | 1.47× | +0.22 |

| sub-period gross Sharpe | full book | intra-equity |
|---|---|---|
| 2000–2012 | **0.56** | 0.23 |
| 2013–on | **0.12** | 0.20 |

On this cross-asset panel the "low-beta half" is mostly **TLT/IEF/GLD plus defensive sectors** — so
the levered long leg is half a duration/gold position, and the gross book moves with TLT (+0.55).
That re-reads the apparent decay: the full book's slide from 0.56 to 0.12 tracks **the end of the
bond bull market** (capped by 2022), not a fading equity anomaly — the intra-equity book never had
the early 0.56 to lose (0.23 → 0.20, flat and small). F&P sort *within* an asset class for exactly
this reason; build it the way they do and what remains here is a steady, modest tilt that the
financing sweep above still erases.

## The honest takeaway

Betting against beta is a `WEAK` real tilt that, priced as the self-financed book it actually is,
**trails the market gross** (0.32 vs 0.48 excess-of-cash) and needs ~2.8× leverage to be
market-neutral — so realistic financing spreads make it a `MIRAGE`. The "low-risk free lunch" is
`BUSTED`: you pay for it in borrow, and the years when it looked best were substantially a levered
bond-bull trade. (A caveat held openly: a finer single-stock universe gives BAB more intra-equity
beta dispersion than 10 sector/region ETFs; the *mechanism* — the edge is the leverage rent — is what
generalises, and it is what kills the headline.)
